papers.title: To predict or to persist: how decoherence shapes learning in a spin-qubit quantum reservoir
papers.abstract: In this work we investigate how dephasing and the choice of measured observables affect learning in a simulated six-qubit spin chain with Markovian dissipation and exact expectation-value readout. For externally driven nonlinear autoregressive moving-average signals, combining single- and two-qubit observables gives better predictions than a population-only readout at comparable polynomial feature counts. Most of the configurations we tested become more accurate than a reference with relaxation and dephasing disabled, most strongly at $T_2=1\,\mu$s, where total memory capacity drops, and still at $T_2=5$-$10\,\mu$s, where memory is only redistributed across delays. For autonomous generation, we train the readout with scheduled sampling and iterative dataset aggregation to expose it to states reached under its own feedback. We do not find a clear systematic dependence of limit-cycle persistence on coherence across the reservoir ensemble. For chaotic forecasting, in contrast, prediction horizons at $T_2=1\,\mu$s shorten in all 10 reservoir realizations relative to that reference. For the noise-driven strange non-chaotic attractor, the model produces a smooth, approximately closed orbit, and neither captures the target's scatter nor follows its trajectory pointwise. We conclude that, within this simulated reservoir, the impact of coherence depends strongly on the task.

papers.title: Large deviations, effective dynamics, and dynamical phase transitions in random maps
papers.abstract: Large deviation theory provides a natural framework to characterize rare fluctuations of time-averaged observables in deterministic and stochastic systems. Building on previous results for deterministic chaotic maps, here we extend the Doob transform to random maps, constructing an effective dynamics in which rare events become typical. This makes it possible to directly reproduce the dynamics of rare trajectories that are exponentially difficult to sample under the original dynamics. We further apply spectral large-deviation methods to characterize dynamical phase transitions in random maps. The spectral structure of the tilted operator provides insight into the mechanisms underlying these transitions and, in particular, allows us to identify the appropriate initial states that select one dynamical phase or another. Our results extend the connection between large deviation theory, spectral methods, and effective dynamics to random chaotic maps, providing a general framework to study rare events and dynamical phase transitions in these systems.

papers.title: Complex chaotic Boltzmann machines as deterministic representations of quantum states
papers.abstract: Neural networks and tensor networks have opened new ways to explore quantum systems by parameterizing families of wave functions through the structure and parameters of a network. Here we extend this perspective to a dynamical representation: we introduce a complex chaotic Boltzmann machine that assigns a deterministic system to a pure quantum state. We extend Suzuki's construction to incorporate both Born probabilities and relative phases. The probabilities set the trajectory velocities in a hypercube, while the phases define a complex field that lifts its Poincare sections. The evolution is determined by the network parameters and initial conditions, without random choices during flights or configuration changes. Our analysis of two qubits and study of three-qubit families show how relations between probabilities organize regular curves, islands, and unstable regions, and how phases distinguish states that share the same Born dynamics. This architecture turns a wave-function parameterization into a geometry of trajectories, providing a tool to explore probabilities, phases, and symmetries together across families of states.

papers.title: Onset of quantum chaos in a family of two-dimensional conformal field theories
papers.abstract: We exhibit random matrix statistics in the scaling dimensions of non-BPS primary operators in a family of two-dimensional conformal field theories. Specifically, we consider the sigma model with K3 target space and $\mathcal N=(4,4)$ supersymmetry in a neighborhood of the Kummer orbifold point $\mathbb T^4/\mathbb Z_2$. At the free-fermion radius, the spin-zero spectrum of the $\mathbb Z_2^4$-invariant sector is exactly degenerate at integer energies. The exactly marginal blow-up deformations that preserve this symmetry form a four-dimensional space, whose directions we parametrize by unit quaternions. Along each deformation direction, we compute the first-order splitting of the degenerate levels, i.e., the leading anomalous dimensions as the coupling goes to zero. In sectors where all exact symmetries are resolved, including a hidden $\mathbb Z_2$ at the even levels, the non-zero first-order shifts along a generic direction follow the Gaussian orthogonal ensemble (GOE), as we verify by computing several spectral diagnostics. We compare quantitatively with the well-known singlet deformation, which has enhanced symmetry: even after all its known symmetries are resolved, its first-order spectrum has exact degeneracies, its gap ratio approaches the GOE value only slowly as the energy increases, and its unfolded spectrum lacks the long-range rigidity of the GOE.

papers.title: Analog Explorations of Quantum State Measurement
papers.abstract: The awkward disconnect in the postulates of quantum mechanics between the continuous, deterministic, linear, and unitary evolution governed by Schr\"odinger's equation and the discontinuous, stochastic, nonlinear, and nonunitary measurement process has vexed physicists for decades. Intuition from classical mechanics, statistical mechanics, and dynamical systems theory suggests that such a process might be modeled with a nonlinear system of differential equations. We explore such approaches by designing a deterministic model of an ideal projective measurement on a single qubit and constructing an analog computer that simulates it by manipulating voltages in an electrical circuit. The model reduces to Schr\"odinger evolution when no measurement is taking place. During a measurement, a hidden variable that the observer does not resolve selects the outcome, and the model is constructed so that a uniformly distributed hidden variable yields Born-rule frequencies. We do not derive the Born rule; rather, we show that a deterministic dynamical system with no intrinsic noise can implement it. Over 300 trials, the circuit reproduces the ideal model's individual outcomes to within one percent of the decision threshold, and its outcome frequencies match the Born rule to within about 0.02 in probability. These results are a small but provocative step towards modeling quantum measurement with macro-scale machines---a step of interest for both the foundations of physics and the alternatives to digital computing it suggests.

papers.title: Learning effective stochastic predator and prey dynamics across physical and biological systems from limited data
papers.abstract: Constructing an effective low-dimensional stochastic model from sparse observations requires separating deterministic drift from state-dependent fluctuations when the governing interaction law is unknown. We formulate an adaptive neural stochastic differential equation with topology constraints (TC-AdaNSDE) for two-variable predator--prey dynamics. To regularize the inverse problem when data are scarce, the model combines flexible drift and correlated diffusion fields with density-adaptive local Kramers--Moyal moment estimates and soft phase-space constraints reflecting boundary saddle behavior near extinction and local stability near coexistence. Using a known nonlinear stochastic system, we first show that short-time trajectory error cannot assess diffusion accuracy on its own and must be paired with distributional measures of one-step transitions and long-time phase-space occupancy. We then apply this framework to macroscopic turbulence and zonal flow energies reduced from Hasegawa--Wakatani plasma simulations and to short ecological time series. In the sparse-data regime, TC-AdaNSDE reproduces both short-horizon evolution and long-time invariant energy distributions where deterministic reductions collapse and unconstrained stochastic fits diverge, while recovering physically interpretable drift and fluctuation fields across both physical and biological systems.

papers.title: A sliding mode observer perspective on chaos synchronisation of turbulent flows
papers.abstract: State estimation of turbulent flows is challenging as infinitesimal prediction errors grow exponentially due to chaos. However, when signals from one chaotic system (the master) are injected into an identical system with different initial conditions (the slave), the slave can synchronise with the master --- a phenomenon observed in turbulent flows. From a control-theoretic perspective, this synchronisation problem can be viewed as observer design. We first show that synchronisation by direct substitution of observed variables into the slave system is equivalent to a sliding mode observer. This perspective enables the analytical verification of stability as well as the design of feedback for robustness. We focus on reduced-order Navier--Stokes models with quadratic non-linearities, a broad class of systems for which stability can be analysed by seeking Lyapunov functions through parameter-dependent linear matrix inequalities solved via semidefinite programming. Extending this framework, we develop a neural network approach combining a neural ordinary differential equation with a decoder to learn data-driven mappings from observation histories to companion forms, where observer design is greatly simplified. Results are demonstrated on the Lorenz system and a nine-dimensional reduced order model of a turbulent shear flow. This work opens opportunities in the rigorous development of observers for turbulent flows.

papers.title: The Geometry of Predictive Precision: Optimal Allocation and Attainable Gain
papers.abstract: A finite-time prediction can amplify small initial errors very differently across state-space directions. Which directions deserve precision depends on both the dynamics and the terminal quantity of interest. We minimize task-weighted terminal error over local covariance shapes of fixed generalized volume. The unique optimum is the inverse of a predictive metric obtained by pulling the terminal requirement through the tangent map; it equalizes propagated uncertainty in the required terminal metric. A spectral expression gives the gain over uniform allocation. We then distinguish two constraints with different physical consequences: limited anisotropy caps the gain, while coordinate-diagonal allocation can lose almost all the benefit if sensitive directions are rotated away from accessible axes. Under dominant finite-time stretching and a fixed anisotropy cap, optimal allocations for different terminal requirements also approach a common shape. Standard-map and double-pendulum examples, together with a direct finite-amplitude check, illustrate these effects. The resulting criteria guide task-aware sensing, state encoding, and precision-controlled simulation by identifying when accessible directions matter as much as nominal resolution.
